latest.summary: Approving an AI service is only the starting point. As employees adopt Claude and their responsibilities change, security teams need to know who has access, which users hold administrative privileges, and whether those roles and group memberships still reflect the work they do. IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that, among studied organizations reporting an AI-related breach, 97% lacked proper AI access controls. The finding highlights a broader challenge: AI adoption needs security practices that extend beyond the initial approval, supported by information teams can use to review access with administrators and service owners. Rapid7 Surface Command now integrates with Claude’s Compliance API, bringing supported organization, user, role, group, and settings information into the same platform teams use to understand other assets and identities. The integration helps security teams make enterprise Claude access part of their existing review practices. Bring enterprise AI access into your security view An account list tells security teams who is present, while roles and group memberships help explain how access is organized and where further review may be needed. Surface Command’s integration with Claude’s Compliance API brings together: Organizations and users: Visibility into the Claude organization and its associated user accounts. Roles and groups: Context to understand users’ assigned roles and group memberships. Organizational settings: Available configuration information to support review of the enterprise Claude environment. With those details in Surface Command, practitioners can examine Claude identities alongside the other assets and identities they manage. That gives them a clearer basis for working with service owners to evaluate whether access remains appropriate as teams and responsibilities change. The integration focuses on administrative visibility. It does not ingest Claude conversation content, provide threat detection on Claude activity, or control Claude’s behavior. From a user record to an informed access review Consider a security practitioner reviewing administrative access to Claude. In Surface Command, they can inspect an imported user’s details, review their organization role and administrative status, and examine their group memberships. The relationship graph provides a visual view of how that user connects to the organization and its groups, making those associations easier to follow. The practitioner can then work with the service owner to confirm whether administrative privileges are still needed, whether group memberships reflect current responsibilities, and whether those assignments align with the organization’s access model. Surface Command provides information to support the review, while the team applies its policies and judgment to determine whether a change is needed. Support AI adoption with clearer accountability As Claude becomes part of everyday work, reviewing its users and access relationships becomes part of managing the environment. Bringing that information into Surface Command helps security practitioners and service owners work from a shared understanding of assigned roles and group memberships. It supports more informed access decisions and helps security leaders incorporate enterprise AI into established oversight practices. Get started with Claude and Surface Command today The integration is available through the Anthropic connector in the Rapid7 Extension Library. Using Claude’s Compliance API requires a Compliance API key and the appropriate entitlement for your Claude organization. Visit the connector page to get started and see how Surface Command brings Claude users, roles, and group relationships into view.

hottest.summary: Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet’s report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request. If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability.
